maintopic: OFFICIAL REPORT OF DEBATES
OFFICIAL REPORT OF DEBATES
speechtext:
I beg to
present the first report of the select standing committee to supervise the official report of Debates as follows:
Your committee have had referred to them for consideration a communication from the King's Printer, submitting the proposed scale of rates hereto appended to be charged for the printing of special editions of speeches of members in the House of Commons.
Your committee have also considered a report from the Printing bureau showing a net loss to the government in the printing of said special editions of speeches at present rates.
Your committee, realizing in view of the increased cost of paper, the necessity of making a slight increase in the rates for the printing of said speeches, recommend that the rates set forth in the scale hereto annexed be approved, said rates to take effect at the opening of the next session of parliament and remain in force until otherwise ordered by the House. (The scale of rates referred to will be found in the Votes and Proceedings of this date.)
Your committee have had under consideration certain irregularities in the distribution of the unrevised edition of the debates to the members of the House of Commons owing to the absence of any fixed rule adopted by your committee and approved by the House.
Your committee recommend that beginning with the opening of the next session of parliament and until otherwise ordered by the House, each member of the House of Commons be supplied without charge with ten copies of the unrevised edition of the debates, four of said copies to be delivered, as at present, and six of said copies and no more to be mailed by the King's Printer to any six persons, companies, corporations or institutions within Canada, whose
[Mr. Meighen.)
names and addresses shall be supplied by such member to the Clerk of the Debates committee.
Your committee have had under consideration certain recommendations providing for a wider and more general distribution of the unrevised editions of Debates at the actual cost of the extra printing, paper, binding and mailing, which has been ascertained to be approximately three dollars per session.
Your committee recommend that the required steps be taken by the proper officers to inform the general public that the said unrevised edition of the debates is available to subscribers, and will be mailed to them daily, upon application to the King's Printer, at the said rate of three dollars per session.
Your committee took up for consideration and report certain matters concerning Hansard which were recently discussed in the House of Commons without formal reference to your committee, but doubt was expressed concerning the powers of your committee to deal with and report upon said matters.
Your committee, therefore, recommend that they be given power to consider the following questions and report their opinion thereon to the House, viz *
1.	Whether Hansard should be a record of debates only, containing such items of the proceedings of the House as may be necessary to make the report of the debates intelligible, or whether it should contain all of the proceedings of the House and of the Committee of the Whole House as well as the record of debates.
2.	Whether it is desirable, in the interests of economy of time, labour and expense, that the report of the debates in Hansard should be limited to such speeches as may be delivered when Mr. Speaker is in the Chair, with or without a brief report of proceedings in committee.
Whether it is desirable to make Hansard an official record of all the proceedings of the House of Commons, as well as a record of the debates.
The whole respectfully submitted.
Geo. H. Boivin,
Chairman.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA

speechtext: The House resumed from June 27 consideration in committee of Bill No. 47 to incorporate the United Church of Canada-Mr. Forke-Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
When the committee
rose we were considering an amendment moved by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) to section 10 (a). The amendment was, to add thereto, in the 33rd line after the word "thereat" the words "or by ballot under the provisions of schedule D." A copy of schedule D is said to be on the desk of each member of the House. The question is on the amendment.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
This point was discussed
to some extent on Friday afternoon last, and I entertained a hope that in the interval the hon. gentleman (Mr. Forke) who is promoting this bill would see the reasonableness of the request of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and agree to the amendment, if not in its exact terms then to a properly drawn amendment that would carry out the intention of the mover. As regards its drafting, the amendment is of sufficient consequence to enlist the services of the law clerk of this House. What we all want is as perfect a bill as possible. I realize that in the drafting of this amendment there may be some difficulties which will require skilled draftsmanship to overcome, but the principle, I submit, should be adopted. We can then leave the drafting over probably until to-morrow or next day, and pass the bill. Apart from this clause, I doubt if there is any other contentious clause in the bill. The principle has now been accepted, and the bill might go through. But this clause is vitally important. The clause as drawn provides that non-concurring congregations shall attend at a church meeting and there decide whether they are to continue their existence as such church, or merge in the union body; and, as was pointed out by the member for Lunenburg, there would be a large proportion of the membership of each individual church not in attendance at that meeting, and consequently those members would be deprived of a vote.
What strikes me as most important is that when this question was twice submitted to the Presbyterian church,-as I know; I do not know how it was submitted to the other

churches-it was on both occasions submitted by ballot. Members of the church could deposit their ballots during the course of a couple of weeks with the proper authorities, and those votes were counted. That is the method adopted by the church itself. Now when it comes to the vital point whether action shall be taken one way or the other, the bill takes away the right to vote by ballot and compels attendance at that particular church meeting. What will be the result? A large number of those who have to be away from home from time to time during the week or during the month will not be entitled to vote; that class embraces railway men, lumbermen, fishermen, travellers, students-a large number in our community are attending the universities-the sick, the aged and the infirm. The bill proposes to practically deprive all these classes of a vote upon this important question. When the matter was up on Friday last I tried to elicit from hon. members who support this bill some valid reason why the clause should be adopted. In my judgment none was forthcoming. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) gave a sort of hazy intimation that there might be some bad work in connection with the ballots; he did not seem to be able to trust the people in the various churches to take a ballot vote. The only other objection urged at all upon the point was that some of the provincial legislatures had already passed bills containing a clause of this kind. What matters it to this parliament if a provincial legislature makes a mistake; are we going to be bound by it? Are we to have the rights of this parliament circumscribed simply because a provincial legislature has passed legislation concerning which we have never been consulted? If such other acts have been passed, that circumstance should not tie our hands. Let us do what is right, and if the ballot principle is right, let us adopt it. Then the parties interested might go to the legislatures and have the provincial legislation amended in this respect.
I do not want to use strong language, Mr. Chairman, but in my judgment it would be nothing short of an outrage to impose attendance at a church meeting as a condition to voting on this great question, when we know, if we know anything, that we are going to deprive a tremendous number of the members of the various churches of the right to vote at all through quite unavoidable absence.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
Might not members on
both sides, unionists as well as non-unionists, be deprived of their votes?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am not taking sides;
I do not want to deprive any church member

United Church oj Canada
of his vote, I want to enable every church member, whether for or against, to have an opportunity to vote. We have no right to assume that one class is going to be away and the other at the meeting. No doubt the deprivation will cut both ways, but surely we should furnish ample opportunity for everyone interested to vote.
Now, there is another objection, and a real objection too. We want to have the vote as free, as unbiased, as uninfluenced as possible, and I do not believe you can get a free, unbiased and uninfluenced vote when the voter has to come and stand in front of his parson and declare himself. I think we recognize that in every country there is such a thing as clerical influence. I know that in the Dominion Elections Act we had a clause which recognized this and provided that clerics were not to be allowed within one hundred yards of the polling booth on election day except to cast their votes.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: That was in 1917.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
It is many years ago,
But here the effort seems to be to bring the voters together under the eye of the parson and dragoon them into voting in the way the parson wants 'them to vote; while the object should be to make the vote a<s free, as unfettered, as uninfluenced as it is possible to make it. Oh, I have heard my hon. friend from Brandon refer almost every week to the fact that this is a progressive generation, a day of progress. But what are we doing here? We are turning our back on progress. The whole world knows from experience that the fairest vote is the vote by ballot.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that ballots are taken in church courts?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I do know that in the election of eldeTS in the Presbyterian church where I attend they vote by ballot and allow you two weeks to turn in your ballot. I never attended a church court, nor have I ever read the rules, so I cannot give any information on that point. But I do know that the experience of every civilized country in the world has .been in favour of the ballot in order to obtain a fair, free and uninfluenced expression of public opinion. By the ballot you get away from influence, you get away from domination, whether it be the domination of the boss, the employer or the parson. And if we want a free vote, why should we turn our back on these yearn of progress, why should we retrace our steps and adopt this high old Tory principle of the open vote? That is what you are now attempting to do, you, ithe great Progressive party in the House of Commons. Until someone can produce some weighty reason for changing the recognized principle of the ballot, I think the clause as drawn should be resisted. My suggestion is this:	Pass this
bill, and let the Clerk endeavour to draft an amendment in lieu of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff). I have looked over his schedule D and I think his provisions in regard to the actual vote and the counting of the vote are excellent. But just these words at the beginning, do not, I think, apply to the whole of the bill. The amendment as drawn is that paragraph (a) be amended by adding thereto after the word "thereat" in the 33rd line of page 6 of the bill the words, "or by ballot under the provisions of schedule D." That is an alternative which would be of no avail: If the meeting is to decide whether the vote be taken by ballot or by attendance at the church meeting, why, you have the same difficulty. The meeting will be there under the eye of those who. in many instances want the vote to go one way or the other, and it will be decided at that meeting whether the vote shall be an open vote or shall be taken by ballot. The procedure should be uniform in all cases; and the reasons for taking a vote by ballot are so strong in this instance that the suggestion made ought to be adopted.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: Would the preacher have any influence on my hon. friend as to how he would vote?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I did not think about
that. I said I have not a vote but that I have in my family five votes, and if the meeting were held in the winter only one of those votes would be registered because four of those persons would not be at home. Why should they be deprived of a vote?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
It is very refreshing to
hear the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) telling this parliament to get away from old Tory ideas and adopt Progressive ideas. I like that, and I am quite prepared to do it at any time. He makes a plea for fair play in the taking of this vote. At first glance his argument seems reasonable, but when you look into the matter you find objections to the taking of the vote in the manner prescribed by the amendment. The amendment provides that the ballot shall be delivered by the clerk of session, the recording steward or the minister. Can you imagine the minister personally delivering the ballots to the members of his congregation without having some influence on those people with respect to the manner in which the ballot shall be marked? That is
United Church oj Canada

one thing that the hon. member is afraid of: that the minister may have undue influence in this matter if the vote is taken in the church. But if the minister delivers the ballot to the members of his congregation he has a very good opportunity to do a little canvassing. So also has the clerk, and so has the recording steward. Then we are told that a copy shall be mailed to the last known address of the members who are entitled to vote by ballot and that an accurate list shall be kept of those who receive the ballots. Then, at a meeting of the session or quarterly board the minister, the clerk of session, or recording steward, shall produce all the envelopes containing the ballots-the envelopes have previously been marked with the name of the person to whom it is to be returned- count them and make a statutory declaration as to the number of ballots for and against. There is also a clause in this amendment that failure or omission strictly to observe any of the regulations prescribed shall not nullify the vote. In other words, no wandering away from the direct provisions of this amendment would nullify the vote, and any question in that respect is to be decided by appeal to the county court or superior court. Now, this seems not too bad if one does not go deeply into the matter. But the taking of the vote will extend over a couple of weeks, and if one side starts a vigorous campaign on its own behalf, the other side will be compelled to take a similar course, and we will have the spectacle all over this Dominion of church people waging a contest among themselves as is done in a political election. An hon. gentleman says. "No." But suppose he is on one side and' I am on the other; if he fights vigorously for his side I should be prepared to do the same for mine, and why shouldn't we? But it is not in the interests of church work or in the interests of the United church or the Presbyterian church that this should take place. I have no objection to a ballot vote taken at a church or congregational meeting. I believe in a ballot vote; probably it is the right way to take the vote. But if the vote is taken at the church meeting both sides have an equal opportunity; one has no advantage over the other. Everyone I am sure, who is sincerely interested in this matter will be out to vote. The people I am afraid of are the people who have no definite opinions, who are indifferent, who can be influenced by canvassing, or whose vote one way or the other can be obtained by simply going after it as in the case of a political election. I would rather see such [Mr Forked
people left out; I would rather have the decision of men like the hon. member for Lunenburg, who is in earnest on one side, and others who are equally in earnest in their advocacy of church union than the vote of a great many people whose votes will be got but who do not really care anything about the matter. I want to see fair play. I am thoroughly in sympathy with those who are anxious that this church union question shall be decided without any hard feelings. I assure the hon. member for Lunenburg that I have nothing but the kindliest feelings towards him and the steps he has taken. I should like to have been able to agree to his amendment just to show that we are willing to meet him so far, but candidly I cannot do so, because I think it would not be in the best interests of all the churches, union or Presbyterian. In regard to provincial legislation there is a question which complicates matters; the passing of this amendment would further make trouble in that, direction. However, I leave that to be debated by those who are better acquainted with the legal technicalities than I am. I cannot see my way clear, Mr. Chairman, to support the amendment.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: Is it the principle of the ballot that the hon. member opposes, or merely the provisions set out in schedule D? Those provisions might be changed. If my hon. friend is also of the view that the vote should be taken by ballot, then we could agree as to the conditions surrounding the taking of the ballot; if they are too drastic as proposed, let us modify them. Does the hon. member accept the principle of the ballot?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: I made it very plain that I would accept the principle of the ballot provided that ballot was taken at a congregational meeting.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
It cannot be seriously argued that the views of those entitled to speak on this question, in the Presbyterian church or any other church, should not be taken by ballot. I understand the hon. member (Mr. Forke) however, to say that while he concedes that principle, he is of the view that everybody must go to the church meeting before he can express his views by ballot. There is a class of people whose opinions on this question seem to have been disregarded by those who are promoting the legislation, and that is the older men and women whose devotion to the Presbyterian churdh has been an integral part of their lives. Many of these people may be ill or otherwise unable to attend a meeting called for the

United Church of Canada
taking of the vote; is it reasonable that they should not be permitted to express their views? It is of no use to concede the principle of the ballot and then add that if certain members of the church are unable to attend the meeting called for the purpose of taking the ballot, their voice shall not be heard.
Take the case of the men in my constituency who work in the coal mines. I know many worthy sons of the church who work in the coal mines in Nova Scotia; and the same is true of the men who 'work in the steel lurnaces. Many of them work at night. And my hon. friend would say that before they can be permitted to express their opinion on the question of union they must give up their work at night. That is manifestly unfair. It is no use for the promoters of this bill to pretend to the committee and the House and the country that they want to accept the ballot principle, and then proceed to make it absolutely nugatory, or if not going that far. to refuse to include in this bill any provision with regard to an expression of opinion by the ballot. I think the suggestion of my hon. friend from South Wellington is very fair and reasonable, and I appeal to those who are promoting this legislation, in view of the fact that as a result of the vote of two or three nights ago the attitude of the House is pretty well understood, to be at least fair in regard to the minority. If the minority in the Presbyterian church, who believe with the greatest possible sincerity and earnestness in the rightness of their attitude on this question, are to be told, when it comes to a question of giving them an opportunity of expressing an opinion in regard to this matter, that they are not to have the use of the ballot, which every hon. member of this House would insist upon in regard to the most ordinary election that takes place in this country-

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: Would the hon. member be willing to extend this method of voting to Dominion and provincial elections? There you vote by ballot, but you must appear in person at the poll.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
(Waterloo):	Would the
hon. member be in favour of the suggestion of the hon. member for South Wellington, to strike out the word "or" in the proposed amendment? Otherwise, would it not be rather an autocratic position for parliament to take?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
In reply to
my hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) all I am asking is that the principle of the ballot as a means of an expression of opinion should be recognized by this House. My hon. friend asks if I would 241
go further and say that people should not necessarily have to go to the polls on election day. I certainly would not say that. The case is entirely different. At a Dominion or provincial election the polls are open from early morning until late at night, and there are special polls held before election day for those who Eire compelled by their duties to be away from home on polling day, in order that they might have an opportunity of expressing their opinion. In British Columbia there is the system of absentee voting, which has hung up the result of the last provincial election for several weeks. So my hon. friend will see that there are ample provisions in the law for the recognition of the rights of those who cannot be at a particular place on a particular day, and what I am saying now is that there should be some recognition in this bill of the situation of the men who perhaps might not find it possible to be at a certain place between seven and eleven o'clock in the evening of a particular day.
In reply to the question of my hon. friend from South Waterloo, in my judgment what we ought to provide in section 10, is not an alternative method, but we should provide compulsorily that the vote shall be by ballot. I agree with the suggestion of my friend from South Wellington that the Law Clerk of the House of Commons should be asked to draw a proper amendment for the purpose of expressing the intent of the committee on that point.
In regard to the question of conflict with provincial legislation, in view of the fact that there may be in some provinces a provision in regard to the method of voting, I would point out that in some of the provinces adherents have the right to vote, and yet here we do not propose to give them the right to vote.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: That is not the point we are discussing.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: If my hon. friend will follow my argument, my hon. friend from Brandon says that we must not provide for voting by ballot because in some of the provinces that is not the method provided, but yet he is perfectly willing to consent to a clause which may prevent adherents from voting, although in certain provinces adherents have the right to vote.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: That is not correct.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
Certainly it
is.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
That will be taken care
of under subsection (b).

United Church of Canada

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: I am pointing out the inconsistency of my hon. friend from Brandon when he raises the difficulty of conflict with provincial legislation. Surely if in certain provinces adherents have the right to vote, as they undoubtedly have in many provinces, the natural argument would be that we should give them the right to vote in this bill.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I think that is provided
for in subsection (b).

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am not
discussing that particular point except for the purpose of showing the inconsistency of my hon. friend from Brandon on the question of conflict with provincial legislation, and the use of the ballot being made compulsory by Dominion legislation.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: I did not say compulsory.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
My hon.
friend indicated that we ought not to provide for the use of the ballot in the way proposed by the hon. member for Lunenburg, because some of the provinces have not provided for the ballot.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: That was not the idea. My idea was that the congregation itself at its meeting should decide whether to vote by ballot or otherwise, leaving it entirely to the congregation to decide.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I quite
understand my hon. friend's attitude, but he mentioned what had been done in certain of the provinces and the desirability of our not doing anything inconsistent with it, and I was endeavouring to point out that he was perfectly willing to be inconsistent in regard to the question of adherents voting under provincial law, and not being allowed to vote under our law. I do not think it is fair that a congregation should decide whether the vote shall be by ballot or not, because supposing the meeting of the congregation is held on a winter night, with the snow three or four feet high; how is any old lady over sixty, or any old man, for that matter, to get to that meeting and express his view?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: My mother is eighty-six and she turned out and voted for me.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
But not on a winter night, with the snow three or four feet deep. That only proves my point. My mother is eighty-three, and she turned out to vote for me, but it was on a nice day in the autumn; I do not know whether she would be able to do it on a winter's night, if there was a snow-storm. My hon. friend would

prevent both his mother and my mother from voting on this church union question, because he will not allow the ballots to be taken home. He does not know whether his mother would not vote against church union. He must not be too sure about it. I think the dear old lady must cherish the church of her forefathers with which she has been associated all her life, and if she had the opportunity of voting by ballot I venture to say she would quietly mark it against church union.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
You think she would
weaken?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I know
what these good old Scottish people feel in their hearts when they are left alone but no matter what their feelings are they would be prevented from expressing them if they had to attend a meeting of the congregation on a stormy winter's night.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext: Why not in the afternoon?

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
I have
pointed out the situation of the working men in that connection.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
They will not be working
on Sunday.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
Some of
them have to. Are we to say that we shall not provide this fair and honest method of obtaining an expression of opinion, but that there shall be some other method adopted under which the meeting would be called by some of those interested at a time when they knew their opponents would not be there? That attitude on the part of those who are imposing this action on the church would be tantamount to saying to the members of the church "We will not give you the opportunity that is afforded by the state in the case of questions even of the smallest possible importance." It seems to me that when the supporters of church union take that position it indicates that those opposed to them are not to be given the fullest consideration. The whole complaint in this matter has been based on the adoption of an attitude of coercion on the part of the so-called majority. WThy should they not be generous in such a matter as this and accede to a reasonable proposition, which no one can question, to be embodied in a properly drawn amendment and incorporated in this bill so that every member of the Presbyterian Church in Canada, where a vote is to be taken on this question, will be given an opportunity, in a manner entirely unfettered, to quietly mark his ballot and indicate his views on this

United Church of Canada
question in the same way as if the balloting was for the election of members to the House of Commons. Surely we ought to throw around the determination of a question of this kind the same reasonable precautions that are extended to the voter when he marks his ballot for an election of a member to the House of Commons.

maintopic: UNITED CHURCH OF CANADA
speechtext:
As a member of the Private Bills Committee I was called upon by my constituency to devote more than ordinary attention to this bill. I have had the honour for a great number of years to represent that constituency in which close upon one-third of the people are English speaking Protestants. They were divided in their opinion upon this bill just as the others are who are interested in this question, but not being a member of any of the churches immediately concerned my sole abject was to try and bring about an understanding such as would promote Christian union generally. I strove to the best of my ability to effect such an understanding. I was in favour of union, and I supported the principles of union in the committee in deference to the request made by a, large number of my constituents; but having received representations from a considerable number of others who are opposed to union I thought I would furnish the dissenters with an opportunity of making good their case. Therefore I supported the amendment that was inserted in the bill. I also had the honour of serving as a member of the sub-committee which sat for two or three days with the idea of trying to bring about an understanding. Having failed in these respects I now appeal to the majority in this the final court of appeal in favour of the idea contained in the amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Duff). In my constituency the chief Presbyterian church is located at New Carlisle, but some of the members of the congregation reside thirty and forty miles away from that town. They are scattered over a long coast line and it would be physically impossible for all these people to be assembled together at a certain date at a specific point to express their views on this important question. In fairness therefore to all parties concerned 

those in favour of union as well as those opposed to it-I think the House would do well to find a means of giving both sides an opportunity of expressing their opinion. We have a rule in politics in this country which is a good one, which has stood the test of time; it is that the will of the majority must prevail. In church matters I presume the same rule will have to apply, although doubt-241J
less there will be dissenters as there always have been. I am old enough to remember when the break occurred in the Presbyterian church in the city of Montreal. I refer to the occasion when Sir Hugh Allan, and other members of the old Scottish Presbyterian church in Montreal refused to enter the Presbyterian Church in Canada, but remained connected with the old Presbyterian Church in Scotland. There will still be a Presbyterian Church in Canada even after the union which this bill accomplishes is brought about. For how long a period this will be no one can tell but it will continue for some time. In the meantime, in the best interests of union, I think all fair means should be adopted, especially in view of the conditions in my own constituency which I have described, to obtain as complete an expression of opinion as possible. It is physically impossible to get all these people, many of them fishermen and lumbermen who are absent from home, together in the one place at a fixed hour

it is out of the question to obtain a complete expression of opinion. Therefore I think the principle of the ballot should be adopted which would be the best means of convincing all parties that the real opinion of the majority has been obtained. What better means could be used than that which is in universal use throughout the country, not only in parliamentary elections but in case of controversies of various kinds and which is secret.? That is a vote by ballot. I think it would be wise on the part of the promoters of the bill to adopt the suggestion that the Law Clerk of the House should be asked to draft a clause for insertion in the bill eo -that when the measure finally passes the House it will have some chance of rallying to its support the majority of those whc are interested in it.

speechtext: The case of the absentee voter of British Columbia has been referred to as an argument in favour of the adoption of the ballot in the present case. M. Macdonald.]
the bill, they excluded that provision. Surely, you can trust the session of the church-I am wdlling to do that in each particular church-to determine the accuracy of the vote and the question whether the party who sends in a ballot has a right to vote or not.

speechtext:
Would the hon. member
favour confining this ballot to those resident in the district? As I understand the amendment now, the ballot would go to those who, perhaps, moved away years before, whose names are still on the church register, but whose homes are permanently somewhere else.

speechtext:
The hon.
member for Lunenburg says that the act provides in the way the hon. member suggests, but not his amendment. I should think that every person who was a regular member of any particular congregation, would have a right to vote in that congregation. Tht course usually adopted in the church is this, that where one is a member of a particular church and moves to some other locality, he takes a certificate from the church with which he has been connected and becomes identified with the church in the locality to which he goes to reside.

Sometimes the names are

I am perfectly willing, and surely my hon. friend is willing to trust the session and elders on that point. I have in my own county a congregation in the country where the people are provided wtih religious services for a distance of ten miles. If a person that lived ten miles away, owing to the day being stormy, or owing to illness, or a death in the family or some other cause was unable to go to the meeting, he would be deprived of his vote. Surely it '}[DOT]* reasonable 'to ask that there be embodied in this bill a provision that every recognized member of the church should be given a reasonable method of expressing his or her view. That is not an unfair proposition. If the promoters of the bill are hopeful of bringing about anything like a union, such as so many of them cherish and conceive is possible, they are throwing very grave and serious difficulties in the way of the attainment of

their object if they fail to give fair play and reasonable consideration to every one who is entitled to vote, to enable him to express his opinion in a well recognized way and in accordance with the practice that has obtained in this and every other institution in the country in the matter of expression of views. I am astounded to think that the promoters of 'this bill should want to adhere to the proposition that nobody shall be allowed to indicate what his views are in regard to this important matter if he happens to be prevented on account of some sufficient cause, from attending a meeting on a certain day. I am sure every hon. gentleman's sense of fair play would at once bring him to consider the reasonableness of the contention that the law clerk should be permitted to draw up a clause which would recognize that principle. 7'hat is all we ask.

speechtext:
There is one phase of the amendment that has not been discussed yet. Under section 3, there are possibilities that should be considered before we come to a decision. This section reads:
The said clerk of session or recording steward. . . .
Which is the same thing;
.... or minister of any congregation in which a vote is to be held shall personally deliver a copy of said ballot to each member of said congregation entitled to vote.
Or he can send it through the mails. If both of those parties happen to be on one side of this question, you will see that they can control the distribution of all the ballots. It may be said that that is not likely to happen. Let me recite my experience. Some citations of a similar nature have been given this afternoon. In our congregation, the clergyman and clerk of session were such strong Presbyterians that they felt satisfied that that was the only route to eternal glory. Imagine the ballots being in their control!

If we are going to seed the countryside down with ballots in this fashion, they should be distributed equitably on both sides of the question. Take the illustration I have given. The clerk of the session was an excellent man and so was the minister, but under this proposed system they would have had all the ballots. Imagine such a condition of affairs! In order to have a fair expression of opinion and an equal opportunity given to both sides, perhaps the ballots should be divided fifty to one side and fifty to the other. There might be something in that, but why depart from the systematic method of doing such things? There are three or four distinct reasons why this amendment should not be adopted. In the first place, it is diametrically opposed to practice of the church itself. It is true that in the case of elders, they may be selected by the method of distributed ballots, but in many places, particularly in rural parts, the elders are selected right at the meeting. But before a ballot can be taken, a congregational meeting has to be held to nominate those elders, and consequently, this is diametrically opposed to the recognised way of doing business.
It is also diametrically opposed to the provincial legislation which has already been passed in six of the provinces. I think somebody has made the remark: What of that? Is this House going to override the will of the provincial houses in the matter of the ballot? I do not think that is contemplated. What is the other alternative? You are going to have two systems of election, and if we are going to be law abiding people, we shall have to abide by both of them. We shall thus have an election under the provincial law, the

regular system that has been the rule of the church as long as I can remember. We disagreed on the former methods. We said, "Let us have all things done decently and in order", and we borrowed a ballot box from the municipality; we had a returning officer and a polling place and got a decision, and it was all over.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext:
Resolved by the	House of Commons,-
That it is expedient that section ninety-one of the British North America Act, 1867, be amended by adding thereto the following subsection in lieu of that set forth in the address of the Senate and House of Commons to His Majesty the King, adopted by the House and Senate, respectively, on the 24th and the 26th June, 1920:-
" 2. An enactment of the parliament of Canada, if expressed to operate extra-territorially, shall have and be deemed to have had, that operation, if and in so far as it is a law for or ancillary to the peace, order and good government of Canada."
And that His Majesty's government be respectfully requested to promote the necessary legislation for the sanctioning of the said enactment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is the adoption of an address to the Imperial parliament for an amendment to the British North America Act making it clear that this parliament has the power to enact legislation with extra-territorial effect

Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction
in matters within its sphere. The question has been much discussed in this country and in the other dominions. It has been recognized that this parliament within its own sphere has all the powers of self-government, exactly as the Imperial parliament has within its sphere, and this opinion is not only admitted by all constitutional authorities but has received the sanction of the highest judicial courts of the Empire. Still, the question whether outside the territory of Canada the legislation of this country has effect or is valid has been discussed, and there has been a marked difference of opinion. The standard opinion, I think, -was the case of McLeod in the New South Wales dominion. It was a case of bigamy, and it was decided by the Privy Council that a citizen of that dominion could not be sued for having contracted a second marriage outside the territory of the dominion because the offence had been committed without the territory and the jurisdiction of New South Wales. The question of bigamy has also been discussed in Canada in many instances. It was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1890, I think, and on that occasion two judges decided that Canada had the full extra-territorial power in respect to its legislation, but three judges decided otherwise. In order to institute proceedings against a Canadian who, already married, goes to another country to contract the second marriage, our section of the criminal code says he must leave Canada with the intent of going to the other place for the purpose of entering into a second marriage; the offence then is committed prior to his leaving Canada.
There have been many cases of bigamy, especially since the war. There have been cases in Montreal of Canadian soldiers who, already married, contracted a second marriage overseas and when they came back were sued for bigamy, but the courts stated that they could not be convicted because the offence was committed outside the territory. In New Zealand there was a case of bigamy in 1919, quite a recent case, in which Chief Justice Stout, stated that the dominion has extraterritorial rights and that the accused should be convicted, but the majority of the Supreme Court of New Zealand decided otherwise, stating that the dominion had no such power. In a Canadian case, that of Keyn versus Attorney General of Canada which went to the Privy Council, the decision was otherwise. It was the case of a man who had entered Canada contrary to the provisions of the Alien Labour Act, and when the immigration authorities instituted proceedings to expel him from the country a writ of
habeas corpus was taken on his behalf and the Canadian judge decided that Canada had no power to expel a man under such circumstances because an extra-territorial effect was involved in the act of deportation. But the Privy Council decided otherwise, namely, that the legislation of Canada in that respect was valid.
Quite recently the question was discussed in connection with mandates given by the League of Nations and by the Peace treaty to South Africa and New Zealand. New Zealand was given a mandate over Samoa and South Africa over German West Africa. In New Zealand the authorities thought they did not have the power to enact legislation for that territory of Samoa, which wras not within their jurisdiction, and they obtained from the Imperial government an order in council giving them such power. South Africa, on the other hand, under General Smuts, contended that they had such power, that they had all the powers of self-government and that that included the extra-territorial effect of their legislation. Their contention was upheld and they legislated for German West Africa, over which they had been given a mandate.
The constitutional authorities allege that there is doubt as to the extra-territorial right of dominion governments. In an article by Sir John W. Salmond who was Solicitor General of New Zealand, he takes the view that the dominions have an extra-territorial power in their legislation. In Canada the question came to the attention of the government in 1920 in a definite manner when the chairman of the Air Board recommended that the government be requested to take the necessary steps to secure legislation by the Imperial parliament provided that any law' of Canada relating to air craft registered in Canada may extend to such air craft and personal license as well without as within the territorial limits of Canada. The House will realize then how important it is that our aviators shall be compelled to follow Canadian regulations even when they are temporarily outside of Canadian territory.
Apart from the necessity for having the ciuestion definitely settled so far as aviation is concerned, there is also the question of our criminal code, especially with regard to bigamy cases, as I set forth a few minutes ago. There is also the question of our customs laws and regulations. Men should not be at liberty to organize conspiracies to defraud Canada while they are temporarily outside of our territory. There is also the

Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction
question of the protection of our coastal fisheries. Indeed, in the Northern Pacific Fisheries Protection treaty we have assumed that we have that extra-territorial right, and the legislation enacted under the treaty assumes that we have that extra-territorial right. Surely it is important for the protection of our coastal fisheries that we should be able to prosecute those who violate our laws and regulations while temporarily outside of the territorial limits. The same thing applies to our shipping regulations, when our vessels are temporarily out of our territorial waters. If this was not clearly recognized it would certainly impose fetters upon the self-governing powers of the Dominion, such as to hamper the natural working of our constitution.
In 1920, parliament unanimously passed a resolution for an address to the Imperial parliament for the purpose of correcting this anomaly, not, I take the trouble of stating again, that we do not contend that we already possess that power; we think we do possess it, but it has been challenged and contradicted by strong constitutional authorities and by many judges, so it is important to have a clear and definite recognition of that right bjr the Imperial parliament.
The amendment which was suggested in 1920 and which was adopted unanimously by '.his House and the Senate provided that:
Any enactment of the parliament of Canada otherwise intra vires shall operate and be deemed to have operated extra-territorially according to its intention in the like manner and to the same extent as if enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom.
The law officers of the Crown in the United Kingdom took some exception to the phraseology of the amendment suggested, and, while I believe they were not right in their contention, thought it might give the parliament of Canada with regard to the other self-governing dominions the same powers as the Imperial parliament has with regard to them. Nobody in this country ever had that intention, and the wording of that amendment clearly could not bear that construction because it stated: "when intra vires," so it could only concern legislation within the power, authority and jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament. There were negotiations between members of the government of the day and the officers of the Imperial government, and a change in the wording was suggested by the law officers of the United Kingdom, which was not acceptable to the Canadian government. Finally, the draft as now proposed has been suggested by the Canadian government. The order in council was passed, I
I Mr. Lapointe.]
think, a year and a half ago, and only recently the Imperial government has signified its willingness to accept this proposed amendment and to have it carried by an act of the British parliament. I repeat, my own view is that the wording of the first amendment is preferable to this one, but this one will give us all that we need and will definitely recognize Canadian rights of self-government extraterritorially as herein defined.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):

speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. Minister of Justice (M"r. Lapointe) for having allowed this resolution to stand over, because I wished to give some expression of my thought with regard to it.
It is not by any means a controversial question. As the Minister of Justice pointed out, the preceding government pdoptedi a resolution in another form, and a form which he thinks is preferable, and now, in consequence of the reasons which he has given us, and which I may say were not known to me before, the resolution appears in a new form.
I know there is one thing the Minister of Justice does not want to do, nor does the government of which he is a member. I am quite satisfied there is no intention in any part of this House to obtain legislation which would enable any possible interference with provincial rights. I am not going to make a charge; I am going to acquit the hon. minister at the same time that I suggest that the particular phraseology gives an opportunity for that. We have under section 91 of the British North America Act general power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada. Then particular subjects are enumerated in section 91; I shall not enter into the category, and by section 92 a limited class of subjects is exclusively assigned to the provincial legislatures. If a thing definitely and actually falls within the categories of section 92, then the Dominion has nothing to do with it, but if it can be said to fall within both, then the jurisdiction of the Dominion is exclusive of that of the province; but there is always a certain jurisdiction on the part of the province that cannot be interfered with by the Dominion, and that ought not to be interfered with.
I think the Minister of Justice will recognize that he is absolutely right in preferring the original draft to the substituted one; the original draft used words to this effect "otherwise within the legislative authority of the parliament." I do not think the British law officers could have taken ob-

Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction
jection to that part of the phraseology. Their difficulty was more probably with the latter part, which said that our legislation was to be effective "to the same extent as if enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom." Probably their objection was to that; but I have not seen the correspondence, and it is not necessary to spend much time on it. I would suggest to the minister that in point of form, yes, and with real substance behind it, it would be well to interpolate in his present resolution the words "otherwise within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada," so that if we are to have extra-territorial powers they shall be limited in terms to the exercise of the powers which are vested in the Dominion, in contradistinction to those vested in the provinces by our charter, which is the British North America Act. I am absolutely sure that the minister has not the slightest intention of going any further, but I think he will see-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext: Will my hon. friend suggest in which way there is a possibility of this interfering with provincial rights?

maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext:
If the minister has not
grasped it yet, I will state it definitely. The moment there is legislation in the words of the proposed enactment I think it is absolutely apparent that we could not interfere with any provincial legislation within Canada, but we could take a provincial subject of legislation and deal with it extra-territorially.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext: The parliament of Canada cannot legislate on subjects that are not within its sphere.

maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

Now, the provinces, it will be said, have no extra-territorial effect to their legislation. That would be the answer that would come to anyone's mind. That is true in a qualified sense but I think it is pretty well established that the provinces have the right to incorporate companies and that while they can only create a company within their territorial ambit yet they may endow it with powers which are capable of being exercised beyond its territorial jurisdiction. That is the result of a series of Privy Council cases decided within the last ten years. That is only one subject that I think of, and the minister will see at once the action that might be taken by some federal parliament in dealing, for instance, with company legislation by the exercise of the extra-territorial power. This
language really sweeps away the limitations between federal and provincial legislation. If you accept that extra-territoriality, then your legislation will be introduced on the ground of extra-territoriality and it would open up a line of argument which none of us in this country,
I think, wants to have opened up. It is so simple and easy to remedy. I think the minister on very slight consideration will see it is advisable to insert these words.

maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

Where would you insert

That would be sufficient "otherwise within its legislative authority."

That is the legislation

maintopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext:
Enumerated under section
91, and any extra-territorial operation should only be given in connection with these classes of subjects. I do not want to talk at much length and, as I say, there is no complaint or controversy in this matter. But the subject is an interesting one and I have been trying to fix in my own mind where we are going to get to by obtaining this power and attempting to exercise it. I followed my hon. friend in his discussion of the bigamy question. That is the principal one in regard to which any difficulty has arisen; but we seem now to have an effective, or a fairly effective way of grappling with that evil because our legislation is good, in the case of a man leaving Canada with the intent of committing an offence. But supposing he does not leave Canada with the intent at all? Supposing he forms the intent, we will say, in a state of the American union; there is a deserted wife in Canada and the man ought to be punished. But if the wrongdoer remains in the United States we are still helpless; we cannot expect extra-territoriality of legislation to be recognized by any foreign power. It can only be within the ambit of the British Empire, otherwise this legislation will have to be followed up by a series of extradition treaties by means of which we could bring out of a foreign country a man who had done the act which we had determined should be a crime even though committed beyond our territorial jurisdiction and these we are not likely to get.	.
The principal point of view I wish to impress on the minister is, that we open up almost a network of conflict with every other British state. If we claim this then all other parts of the Empire can equally claim it; and if it is
3S20

Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction
accorded to us, we assume it will be accorded to all others. Then once you get a citizen of Canada outside of the three mile limit of this Dominion there is a possibility of a number of jurisdictions affecting him. Eor he may go from one part of the Empire to the other and by what law will he be judged if he commits an offence? We read in the Scriptures of St. Paul claiming the rights of a Roman citizen, which brings very vividly before 5 p.m. our minds that which was undoubtedly the principle of the Roman law in early times when a man, so to speak, carried his law with him. But Rome was then the centre of enlightenment, set among a multitude of mere barbarous tribes, and Rome had the power of her legions to enforce her law. Whether it was what we would now call a contract or whether it was a crime the Roman citizen would claim the right to be judged by the law of Rome and by that law only.
_ Put is it possible for us to put the Canadian citizen in that position in all parts of the world, or even in the British Empire itself? If he sets foot in New Zealand he will have to be judged by the local and territorial law of New Zealand; if he sets foot in London he must be judged by the law that obtains at Westminster; if he goes to South Africa the Roman-Dutch law will take care of him both civilly and criminally. Where is our extraterritorial law to operate? It cannot operate in the United States where most of these offences against the law of marriage are committed. It might operate, possibly, on the high seas, but if our citizen is on a British ship he will be then practically within the territory of Great Britain. I see nothing but cross currents of legislation arising out of this. And after all, what has the United Kingdom done itself? Away back, I think about 1878 or thereabouts, there was the criminal case of a man named Keyn who had committed a murder on a foreign ship and outside the three mile limit. The case came before the Central Criminal Court, and it was held the court had no jurisdiction territorially because its jurisdiction stopped at the three mile limit. Great Britain afterwards passed an act, and this seems to be as far as the United Kingdom has attempted to go in the hne of extra-territoriality. The act was passed m 1878 and recited as follows:
Whereas the rightful jurisdiction of Her Majesty tier heirs and successors, extends and has always extended over the open seas adjacent to the coasts of the United Kingdom and of all other parts of He* Majesty s dominions to such a distance as is necessary lor the defence and security of such dominions.
2. An offence committed by n person, whether he is or is not a subject of Her Majesty on the open sea 
within the territorial waters of Her Majesty's dominions is an offence within the jurisdiction of the Admiral, although it may have been committed on board or by means of a foreign ship, and the person who committed such offence may be arrested, tried and punished accordingly.
A requirement was inserted in the act that had reference to any other portion of the Empire that the leave of the government of the particular dominion would be necessary to bring a prosecution. That, I think, in general terms, while Canada is not mentioned, applies to Canada. The reference is unmistakable, and it means that the leave of the Governor General would be necessary to bring about a prosecution under this particular act. The act also defines "territorial" in these words:
" The territorial waters of Her Majesty's dominions " in reference to the sea, means such part of the sea adjacent to the coast of the United Kingdom, or the coast of some other part of Her Majesty's dominions, as is deemed by international law to be within the territorial sovereignty of Her Majesty; and for the purpose of any offence declared by this act to be within the jurisdiction of this administration, any part of the open sea within one marine league measured from low water mark shall be deemed to be open sea within territorial waters of Her Majesty's dominions.
So that Great Britain herself, with all the plenary' power of the Imperial parliament, did not^attempt to legislate any further than a stones throw from her shores, the three-mile limit. Now we are asking that a sort of unlimited extra-territorial jurisdiction be conferred upon Canada. I see only the possibility of conflict. I see the helplessness, the utter impotence on the part of Canada to enforce this extra-iterritorial jurisdiction if it leads into a foreign state, and I see some difficulty in reconciling the conflicting claims of jurisdiction which may be set up" by the several parts of the British Empire. I can see no real, clear good. Constitutionally, our courts have affirmed the right to go as far as we have gone with reference to the bigamy sections of the code. They have done that, over-ruling a very strong opinion by the late Chief Justice Strong. I noticed that the present Mr. Justice Anglin some years ago contributed a most scholarly and valuable article to the Canada Law Times on this subject, and I take it that his opinion would scarcely be in accord with the legislation that we now have on our statute books. I am not going to oppose the resolution. I only want to point out to the minister some of the difficulties which possibly were not laid before him when his department were giving consideration to the framing of this legislation. I would suggest to him that the matter is not one of immediate

Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction
urgency, that he might take time and give some further consideration to this far-reaching subject and not rush into Imperial legislation which may confuse us in a tangle that, in after years, we may have some difficulty in unravelling.

Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to support the view of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in regard to this matter, notwithstanding the very able argument that has been presented to the House by the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter). I remember well when this matter became a real issue, a definite question in this parliament. I happened, at that time, to be chairman of the Air Board and also Acting Solicitor General, and I remember well when we brought the question to the attention of the Hon. Mr. Doherty, who was then Minister of Justice. The question is a large one and one which, I think, it is in the interest of Canada and of all parts of the Empire to have definitely settled. If there is a real doubt as to the jurisdiction of this parliament to act extra-territorially, we should have that doubt removed at the earliest possible moment. It may be, as the hon. member for St. John City has pointed out, that this is not a case of urgency; that we are not bound to act precipitantly. If there are real difficulties in the matter, we shall have plenty of time to consider them; but I think the matter has now been under consideration for at least three or four years between the Department of Justice and the Imperial authorities, and if they have come to some conclusion which is acceptable to both parties, my view is that the matter ought to be settled. It is to be noted that in the drafting of the former address which was passed by this House, provision was made to protect the rights of the various provinces in any jurisdiction which they have exclusively under section 92 of the British North America Act. I cannot remember that the question arose in the discussion of 1920; I am inclined to think that it must have arisen on those words which the hon. member for St. John City has pointed out would not likely have appeared in the address at that time. But I -think the suggestion of the hon. member for St. J-ohn City that those words be included in the present address should be followed. I cannot imagine that the Imperial law officers would take any exception to the words:
Otherwise within the legislative authority of Canada.
being inserted in this resolution. I think, perhaps, on a strict reading of section 2 as now drawn, it might be held that the language means that we could exercise jurisdiction extra-territorially only in regard to such subjects as are placed under the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada by the British North America Act. The inference from the language is certainly very strong. The presumption would be that we were dealing only with such matters in regard to which we had undoubted jurisdiction, but it would make the matter doubly clear if the words suggested by the hon. member for St. John City were included.
Under our criminal code a number of cases arise in regard to which this extra-territorial jurisdiction is very necessary. It is not very long ago when, in my part of the country, there was a rather important case where a conspiracy to defraud was deliberately hatched in Buffalo, by Canadians. They proceeded to Buffalo; they drew their documents there, and entered upon their conspiracy. Afterwards, when they returned to Canada, and were charged in Canada, they were acquitted on the ground that the offence, if any, was committed in a foreign country. If we had had extra-territorial jurisdiction, those men on their return to Canada could have been dealt with under our own law. That is only a single instance but I have no doubt hon. members could recall to mind many instances. There is, of course, the case of bigamy. There are questions arising under our customs laws and the like. I would urge upon the minister to take the question up at once with the Imperial authorities and to see if they will accept the amendment suggested by the hon. member for St. John City. If so, I think we would be justified in going ahead and taking chances in regard to the other difficult questions which might possibly arise at some time in the future. That is only a possibility and, in most instances, a very remote possibility; but in the meantime we are suffering some inconvenience on account of the uncertainty which exists as to the rights of this parliament to legislate now extraterritorially in regard to matters over which it certainly has legislative authority.

I appreciate my hon.
friend's remarks, but I still feel a great difficulty as to how the British parliament can give us any power to legislate extra-territorially except it be within the limits of the British Empire. If people go to Detroit to form a conspiracy, form it and execute it there, I fail to see how the British parliament can
Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction

give us any power to make criminal an act which was committed in Detroit. The British parliament may resolve the rather vexed question in reference to naturalization of aliens. My opinion-and it may not be worth much-is that when we have naturalized a man in Canada, we have made him a British subject throughout the world. The contrary seems to have been held. But even if I am wrong about that, the British parliament could certainly give us power to enact laws which would bind British subjects resident in Canada wherever they might go, and make our law follow them; but that law would only be enforceable when they came within our territorial jurisdiction. That is rather mixing-up two things. We ask to get extra-territoriality for our laws. That cannot be given by any legislative power in the world but we may achieve the same results by treaty. What we may get is a declaration that Canadian laws shall bind subjects of His Majesty resident in Canada wherever they may go in the world. There is a very radical distinction, and I think perhaps the present resolution is climbing up the wrong tree.
