Indian Act Amendment

and Eskimos. One of the chief reasons for bringing the Eskimos definitely under the Indian Act is that at Aklavic at the mouth of the Mackenzie river, where traders from Canada and the United States are active, many of the Eskimos are fairly well off, and it is doubtful whether anyone has jurisdiction over them, although we have been treating them to all intents and purposes as Indians.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Has the minister before
him the definition of Indian in the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, this is the definition:
" Indian " means any male person of Indian blood reputed to belong to a particular band; any child of such person; any woman who is or was lawfully married to such person.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then there is no definition of Indian at all, except that a person to be an Indian must be a member of a band, and, I presume, a band with whom we have made a treaty. Well, the Eskimos go in bands, too. I always regard an Indian as a native of Canada; and the Eskimo is certainly just as much a native in that sense-that he was here before Columbus.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: An aborigine.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes. Consequently he
appears to be covered by the act as much as he ever need be covered. Then I call this to the attention of the minister: we have never made any treaty with Eskimo bands. Personally I do not feel disposed to treat the Eskimos on that basis. My own opinon would be to leave them alone-make them comply with our criminal law and give them all the benefit of our civil law; in other words, treat them as everybody else is treated. I should not like to see the same policy precisely applied to the Eskimos as we have applied to the Indian.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In what particular does my right hon. friend object?

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I object to nursing.
I really think the nursing of our Indians has hurt them. The best policy we can adopt towards the Eskimos is to leave them alone. They are in a latitude where no one will ever bother them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am inclined to agree with my right hon. friend, except that we are forced to assist the Eskimos just as we are forced to assist the Indians. The white man came and took away the Indians' means of livelihood.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
He will never take the
Eskimos'.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is being done at the moment. I am not asking that the Eskimos be placed under the department in order that they may be made wards of the government, nor is it my desire that the effect shall be to make them dependent upon the people of Canada for a livelihood. But white men are going amongst them; the missionaries are beginning to require education for the children, and for that reason I think it is advisable that we have the Indian Act apply to the Eskimos. Of course whether they are under the Indian Act or not, if famine strikes a band of these people we must come to their relief.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is the minister not doing by this section just what he does not want to do, namely, make the Eskimos wards of the Dominion? I do not want to make the Eskimos wards at all, and in that I agree with the minister. Give them all the rights that our Canadians have. There will be no invasion of their domain on our part and there will be very little invasion of ours on theirs if any at all. So far as they want to come, let them come. The minister is also right when he says that if there is a famine we ought to try to help them, the same as we do anybody else in our country, especially the same as we do the aborigines of our country. But do not let us start on the path making them wards. Perhaps the next thing we hear the Eskimos will be over at the League of Nations.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We have
never, so far as I know, entered into any treaty with the Eskimos. They have not been treated as a band, although they actually are a band, with their chiefs, following the Indian mode of life. The white trader is going in among them, so much so that we have been forced to establish police posts in those localities. We must have some regulation by which we can deal with these people, outside of any question of their becoming wards of the government.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister is doing
here just what he said he did not want to do. Let me read the section:
The Superintendent General of Indian Affairs shall have the control and management of the lands and property of the Eskimos in Canada and the provisions of Part I of the Indian Act shall apply to the said Eskimo in so far as they are applicable to their condition and mode of life, and the Department of Indian Affairs shall have the management, charge and direction of Eskimo affairs.

Indian Act Amendment
That simply means that hereafter the Eskimos are to be considered wards of the Dominion, with all the consequences of that relationship. For example, an Indian to-day cannot be sued; an Eskimo can. I do not suppose he ever is, but if this bill passes he never can be. The government is in possession of his property; the government has made him a child. The minister says that left to their own resources some of them are already pretty well off. Well, there are not any Indians very well of, or mighty few.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh yes.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
After seventy-five years
of tutelage and nursing, for the most part they are still helpless on our hands. I do not think we could have treated the Indian differently, and we treat him generously yet. But the Eskimo is different in this regard. The only air he can breathe is the northern air. There is where he is going to stay; there is where we are not going to go in very great lumbers. Let us give the Eskimo the full oenefit of our civil law; if necessary give him the benefit of special precautions to see that he is not imposed on. But I do think we are taking a pretty serious step when by this bill we put our wings all around his property and tell him he is our ward and that we will look after him.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is the
opinion of the officers who have to do with the Eskimos that they would be much better under some such provision as is proposed. There is no doubt that many of them are comfortably off. Some of them own their own fishing boats-and by the way, some of these boats were ordered in Canada this year, costing about $4,000 or $5,000, and were sent north. Of course the Eskimos come under the general law that protects a Canadian citizen, but they do not get the same protection that the Indian Act would provide. If my right hon, friend argues that they should be left as they are, in ownership of their territory, allowing them to protect themselves unless they get into trouble -well, I hardly agree with him. However, I am not particularly anxious to press the bill if there is a feeling that we should not undertake this responsibility and place the matter under the control of some department.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have no objection to
one of the departments having charge of Eskimo affairs, and I have no doubt that the Indian department is the right one, to see that the officers of the law are there, to 242
see that our general civil rights are given them to the full, and to see as well that they are not left to starve; that on the principle of relief, and that principle alone, we may help them the same as any others who are in distress. But what I object to is that we should make the whole population our wards from this day henceforth and make their property legally ours, they simply enjoying the use of it; bringing them into the category of the Indians, with all the responsibility entailed. I think it is a mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would my
right hon. friend be content with the simple statement that for the purposes of administration the Eskimos should come under the control of the Department of Indian Affairs, without any question of taking control of their lands as is provided in this section?

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Well, I am not sure that that would get just what I want.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I was going to ask the
minister a moment ago whether any request had been made to the government by the Eskimos through their chiefs that they be brought within the provisions of the Indian Act. But apart from that I do not think that at this stage the government should bring any persons in as wards of this country. If the Eskimo is the person I understand him to be, any such provision would only make him less ambitious to earn his own living. The Eskimos are a thrifty people, and aside from some unforeseen occurrence, such as the loss of the animals which constitute their crop, they have done about as well as most other people. The next thing we shall have here will be the Doukhobors, if they get into trouble, asking to be brought in as wards of the government. These people are really not natives of Canada; they come in from some other place, and they find that in that part of the country they can eke out a living where they could not do it anywhere else. So far as being imposed upon is concerned, there are many people in this country who are imposed upon, If the Eskimos are in hard luck, if their crops are ruined, the government extends a charitable hand to them, but that is no reason why this government should undertake to make wards of such people. There might be considerable difficulty in doing that. As I understand the provisions of the Indian Act, the consent of the Indians must be first obtained before certain things can be done, especially in regard to property and estates, which are owned by the government.

Indian Act Amendment

I agree with the leader of the opposition that we should have more information upon this question and ascertain definitely why the Department of Indian Affairs wants to pass this amendment. So far as being imposed upon is concerned, perhaps fifty per cent of the people in this country are imposed on at some time or another in matters of trade and business, but that is no reason for making them wards of the government, and I presume the Eskimos are in the same category. I, for one, with the information that is before us, cannot concur in this legislation. I do not think the fact that we have been giving the Eskimos a little charity, and the further fact that they have been imposed upon, is sufficient reason for bringing them under the Indian Act.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I certainly agree with the
remarks of the previous speaker (Mr. Carroll), and also with the argument put i forward by the leader of the opposition. But not only is it a bad thing for us to take the Eskimos on our knee as wards; there is another objection to this clause, perhaps equally as great. What, for instance, are the aboriginal rights of these people? Have they any rights, for instance, to the lands they now occupy? Have they entered into consultation with the Dominion government asking that the Superintendent General should administer their lands? If not, it might only lead to a great deal of trouble if we were to assume the right to administer their lands without consulting with them as to their aboriginal rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friends have the idea that the Eskimo in his habits is similar to the Indian, but this is not the fact. The Eskimo, except in rare cases, does not live in definite localities. He follows his food, wherever it may be. True, he returns to certain points for fishing, and that sort of thing. On the other hand, the Indians from time immemorial had definite localities where they established themselves as tribes. The Hurons and the Algonquins, for instance, all had definite areas in which they lived long before the white man came to Canada. That is part of the difficulty in British Columbia to-day; these various tribes had definite locations which they called their own. But the Eskimo does not follow that mode of life to the same extent, and so far as I know he has not laid claim to aboriginal rights or title to his land. He is established in Aklavik, which is probably the best settled district where the Eskimos congregate, has established his home

there, and undoubtedly through right of tenure could lay claim to that particular locality; but there is the whole of that immense territory in the north over which the Eskimos roam, and to which, just recently, owing to the very great increase in the price of fur, the attention of the white man has been directed. He is trading with them, and is bringing his mode of trade and of life amongst them; there is more contact being had to-day than ever before with the Eskimo tribes in the north. Now, whether or not you strip this amendment of the wording that deals with the land altogether, I do think that some department of the government should be designated to have some supervision over the Eskimo tribes. I am not particular about taking control of the land or bringing them as wards under the control of the government, but whether you do that or not, this government in times of distress must come to the rescue of these people, and in order to avoid that as much as possible, and to prevent disease getting amongst them, if that is possible, it should be made the business of some department of the government to look after these people and render them such protection as the government can afford, for after all they are citizens and natives of that territory, and there is much more trade going on in that territory than ever before.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I appreciate the difference
between the actual position of the Eskimo and that of the Indian, as put forward by the minister, but it is not so fundamental as it would appear. It is agreed, I presume, that the Eskimo is not so definitely fixed at one point, but it is equally true that he is fixed, and very definitely fixed, in a certain latitude, and he looks upon that territory as his home just as much as the Indian looked upon certain areas of this country as his home. I would suggest that the minister take whatever steps are necessary to prevent the white man from robbing the Eskimo, but keep away altogether from taking any control over his land.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We can let
this section stand for re-drafting. I would like to consult with the solicitor of the department and have it re-drafted to cover what appears to be the consensus of opinion of the committee, namely, that it should be just a matter of control, without making a ward of the Eskimo.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister should remember that the distinction that really counts

Indian Act Amendment
is the one that he has not mentioned. In the case of the Indian, there was a certain territory that the Indian occupied and used. We took that territory, and we therefore had to make terms with the Indian. We had to live among him. We could not live among him on an equality, because he was not of a status to warrant it. We therefore made him our ward. There may be some question of the rightness of making him our ward, but it has been done, and we have paid a frightful penalty for it so far. On the other hand, we are not taking the Eskimo's land; we do not need to make any treaty with him. He is in free possession of his territory. It may be he now has facility to sell what he could not sell before, but in so far as that is concerned, it has helped him, and-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
A serious
situation would arise if we got into a dispute over the sale of the territory.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, I would keep away
from that; I would not cross the bridge till I got to it. In the meantime I suggest to the minister that he use the agency we have had all along; I think it is under himself; he is the minister in charge of the Northwest Territories, and has a commissioner there. It would seem to me this commissioner and his organization, very small, if he has any, comes in contact with the Eskimo, and has in the past, and utilizes the mounted police, and this is probably the best means. I fancy the minister's deputy is ill advised in trying to bring in the Eskimo in any special way now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
All I am
asking is that we should settle definitely who is to deal with the Eskimo, because up to now we have been voting sums of money that have been spent upon him, largely for relief purposes, it is true, through the agency of the mounted police. I do not think it would be well to put the Eskimo under the control of the Department of Justice, because as my hon. friend pointed out, the Interior department is in control of the Northwest T erritories.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It should be the Interior department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If it should be the Interior department, I think we should in some way set it out. If it is agreeable to the committee we will let this section stand until I have had an opportunity of discussing it further with the department.
Section stands.
242i
On section 2-Administration of Indian ' estates.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister did not
get through with his explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This is simply to make clearer the action that can be taken in the case of an insane Indian. As my right hon. friend knows, in most of the provinces some individual is appointed by the provincial authorities to administer the estates of insane persons. This legislation will, to some extent, give us control of an insane Indian's estate.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am very much mistaken if the minister has not this power already. In my time we administered the estates of insane Indians. It may have been that something was lacking legally but if so I never knew it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We had not the authority to take the proceeds of any Indian property in order to maintain an insane Indian in a hospital.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Does the minister happen to have a memorandum on this one clause?-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have not
other than what is set forth here. I was looking up the act but I think it is evident the law needs to be clarified in order to enable us to do what we contemplate. The act is not sufficiently clear to enable us to use the proceeds from any property owned by the insane person to maintain him in the hospital. That is all that this provides for.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I certainly have no objection to the power being granted, but I am astonished if it does not already exist. What has been done during the past fifty years? Nobody would suggest that no Indians have gone insane, there have been quite- a lot of them, and we must have been managing their property?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This provision is to make it clear that we can exercise the necessary authority to pay for the maintenance of the insane person.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Inheritance of Indian dying without issue.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I suggest that we call it six o'clock. This clause will take some time because there is quite a lot of explanation required.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

Indian Act Amendment

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The word "Indian" has been struck out in the fourth line of section 28 to enable the nearest of kin who io not happen to be Indians to share in the listribution of the estate of their deceased [DOT]elative who may be an Indian. We have a lumber of mixed marriages amongst the Indians, and whenever an Indian woman marries a white man she ceases to be a member of the band and ceases to have any rights in that connection. If her brother or sister dies possessed of property, this is to enable her to participate in the distribution of that property, the same as other relatives.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Was the last clause in
the act before, the proviso regarding inheritance rights?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Supposing he leaves a
widow not of good moral character, what happens? This act is utterly silent as to what happens then. Who is the judge of her character? Is it the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Usually the Superintendent General is the judge in matters of that kind. The Indian Act gives him pretty wide powers, as my right hon. friend knows.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It seems to me that the
word "such" should be inserted before the word "widow" in the fourth line of section 28:
If he leaves no such widow.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not just follow my right hon. friend there.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As the act reads now, in case an Indian dies leaving a widow of good moral character, she gets his estate. The next clause says that if he does not leave a widow at all, his estate goes to the next of kin. There is still another contingency which is not provided for, that is, if he leaves a widow who is not of good moral character. What becomes of the estate then?
[Mr. Meighen.)

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This discussion seems to be carried on in an amiable but almost inaudible fashion.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is really on a subject that the hon. member should scarcely hear any way. I suggest that he come closer if he is anxious to hear the discussion. The act is in a form in which it should not remain in that respect. If the minister wants to keep it the way it is-and I have no objection -he should insert the word "such" before the word "widow".

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In that regard the wording is the same as in the old section 28. The only amendment we are seeking to make is to bring in relatives of the deceased who are debarred on account of marriage to white persons.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is wholly wrong. The word "such" should be inserted.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Frankly, I
do not see how that is going to change the condition of the widow. She has to be of good moral character now.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There are three events
that may happen. The Indian may leave a widow of good moral character; he may leave a widow of bad moral character or he may leave no widow at all. The first and last are provided for. In the first case the widow gets the estate. In the last, the next of kin gets it, but no provision at all is made for the middle case. There would be if the minister inserted the word "such". Then the next of kin would get the estate. That is what is intended, but the act is silent.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Is it the intention
to debar a widow who is not of good moral character?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There is
no doubt about that, or the words "good moral character" would not have been inserted. As we are letting the others stand, we will let this section stand.
Section stands.
Section 4, sub-section (2)-Powers of superintendent exercised by deputy. When cancellation not invalid or defective.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The explanation simply
reads that section 61, which is the section amended, does not provide as it stands for the observance of any formalities in carrying out the cancellation of a sale or lease for violation of the conditions of such sale or lease. This amendment is to embody in the act what has always been the practice with

Indian Act Amendment
respect to cancellations; that is to say, it is intended to provide a written form which is to be effective for purposes of cancellation. Is this the practice?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is practically following out the provisions of the cancellation proceedings provided in leases in the Department of the Interior. There was a question as to the right or authority under the act of the Superintendent General to cancel. This provision is simply making it clear that he has that authority. A question has been raised as to the delivery of the notice. We have been attacked on two counts, namely that the Deputy Superintendent General had not the power to cancel, and that our notification was not regular; and as there have been a great many cancellations-in fact all cancellations have been made by the Superintendent General-we are making it clear that he has that authority, and validating those cancellations which he has made. We have to read clauses 3 and 4 to get the full sense of the amendment to section 61. While we are doing that we are not affecting any rights of any individual who has entered action prior to May, 1924. This is what we did in connection with the validation of leases in the Mining Act a couple of years ago.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The English seems to be bad. Take the infinitive in the fourth last line-how does that work in as an infinitive? I cannot see it. I will read it aloud so that hon. members will understand it. It says:
For the purposes of this section the powers and authorities conferred upon the Superintendent General shall be and be deemed always to have been exercisable by the Deputy Superintendent General.
That is all right. The section continues:
And in any case where the Superintendent General or the Deputy Superintendent General has heretofore cancelled any sale or lease, or shall hereafter cancel any sale or lease, for any of the causes mentioned in this section, such cancellation shall not be or be deemed to have been invalid, defective, or irregular by reason only of the fact that the purchaser or the lessee, his heirs executors, administrators or assigns, or, if the purchaser or lessee be a corporation, the corporation, its successors or assigns, or any person claiming by, through or under him, it or them, was not notified previously to such cancellation of intention to cancel, or to consider the facts of the case with a view to determining the execution of the power of cancellation.
I can say definitely that it is hopeless. I will not be criticised for using that word again. It makes no sense. To put it. briefly, the section says that, for the purposes of this section, the Superintendent Genera! or the Deputy Superintendent General shall be deemed to have had the power of the minister. That is all right. Then it says that any cancellation previously effected or to be effected shall not be deemed to be invalid because the party whose lease was cancelled got no notice previous to cancellation. Up to that point, whether it is good law or not, it is good sense; but it goes on and says "or to consider." Who is to consider? What does that mean? It does not mean anything. It looks as if it had fallen in from some other act. It has no place there.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is dealing with corporations there pure and simple. It may not be very clear, but we have so many cases in which corporations are interested in these purchases that it is difficult sometimes to know who the parties are. So that it is an endeavour to cover any point that may be raised in connection with the communications with the representatives or otherwise of the corporations. Dealing with individuals it is perfectly clear. My hon. friend will remember that a great many of those agreements of sale are made. The agreement of sale is sometimes sold to somebody else. Perhaps two or three individuals have dealt in this property, and then suddenly they all fail to pay, and, in order to clear up the property we are taking this precaution, and they shall be notified. Then we have the case of the corporation which purchases. Any number of complications arise about the purchase of the property, and we are simply seeking to cover the whole of it.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I see a possible way of
getting the language together, but no way that would make it decent English in that construction. I do not know that anybody is finding fault with what the minister wants to do, but whoever has been employed to put the minister's meaning into English has used neither English nor French, the only two languages recognized in this parliament, and we are not conversant with any other.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It makes no sense at
all. I think I see what the minister is after, but he has not got it. I could not see it for a long while. What is the sense of saying that a cancellation cannot be invalid merely by reason of the fact that the authority cancelled it under notice previously of such cancellation or intention to cancel? The word "of" should be "or"; that is plainly a misprint. It reads "previously to such cancellation of intention." How could you cancel an intention to cancel?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Not having a legal training-
Indian Act Amendment

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: One is better without it in this case. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: - I do not wish to argue it. But I see my right hon. friend's contention.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I wonder these sections are not divided into reasonably short sentences. For instance, this subsection contains nineteen lines, averaging about ten words to a line, or about 190 words. No one but a lawyer has any idea of the beginning of the sentence by the time he reaches the end. I would suggest to the minister that he put this bill into the hands of an ordinary sensible layman instead of a lawyer, to recast it in good English.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then we will have litigation for the rest of our lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Of course, 1 am not a legal draftsman. I will have the subsection re-drafted.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Assuming we have here what the draftsman intended to say, is the minister not going a little too far? I am willing to support him in going to great lengths in validating cancellations the result of mere technicalities, but here he is asking that every cancellation be declared valid even though the purchaser or lessee had not only no notice of it at all, but no notice of intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is not the intention.	*

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But that is what is here.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I admit that on the face of it it appears so. It is very difficult to notify all the interested parties in one of these deals, and your cancellation proceedings may be invalidated by the mere fact that although you have been careful to notify the original purchaser, his equity has disappeared by assignment or otherwise and he is no longer an interested party. What I want is to ensure the purchaser being properly notified, and that is always done, but our [DOT]difficulty is caused by so many transfers having taken place. I am informed that this was drafted by the Department of Justice.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If we are interpreting
a statute in the courts, we cannot say, "Well, parliament intended so and so." The act must speak for itself whether its express words give the intention of parliament or not. I agree with the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) that these lengthy sections should be broken up into various subsections so as to thoroughly convey to the reader what is the intent of the section.

Some people may say, "Lawyers want to becloud the issue in order to get cases." That is not so. Lawyers always know what they are doing. They may disagree at times, and their clients may have to pay for such disagreement, but only after a thorough presentation of both sides of the case. It has been said that when a doctor makes a mistake he buries it;-

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: -but lawyers seldom make mistakes which their clients have to pay for. The average lawyer to-day who has any respect for his profession discourages litigation, for he does not make money by going into court. Therefore statutes should be worded as plainly as possible in order that "he who runs may read". But however plainly the intention of parliament may be stated in a statute, I am sure my fellow-practitioner will agree with me that finally only an intelligent lawyer can interpret its true meaning.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I make this suggestion
to the minister in so far as the wording goes, unless he intends to recast the whole sentence, namely, that after the word "or" he insert the words "of intention," so the sentence will read, "or of intention to consider." Then with a reasonable effort a layman can get at the meaning.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is badly expressed.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not say that that
is the only improvement which might be made, but it undoubtedly would be a very great improvement at the most obscure point. Would the minister also bring a statement from his law clerk, Mr. Williams, as to really all that he intends to accomplish by this section? He is accomplishing so much that he is in danger of simply cutting out the rights of the most bona fide purchasers. According to this subsection he validates every cancellation not only if the interested party got no notice but even though he never knew of the cancellation. The minister says, "Yes, but we do not want to do that; all we want is to see that we are not declaring invalid any sale or lease merely because some one holding shares in a company was not notified." Well, no man because he holds an interest in a company is entitled to individual notice; he never was. There must be some mistake about that. But if there are partners, and they are on record in the department, they are all entitled to notice; and the minister would never ask parliament to pass an act which would declare those partners not entitled

Indian Act Amendment
to notice. I am not at all clear what the departmental officers intend) by this section. If I am clear, and it does not extend too far,
I am prepared to go a long way with the minister to validate cancellations.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is
just possible that the Department of Justice has tried to cover every contingency. All we want to do is to clear up the question whether the Deputy Superintendent General had authority to sign for the department. That is necessary owing to the fact that hundreds of these leases and sales have been cancelled by the action of the Deputy Superintendent General. Then, there is the question of notification. No cancellation proceedings are ever taken until notice has been repeated^ sent to the person in arrears. Some of these sales run over a period of ten years. A short time ago, on the Galician .eserve, we could get no response from two or three parties who were interested in a sale -Americans-although an examination of the files showed that they had been repeatedly notified. The sale was cancelled and the land was subsequently sold, and the parties interested have now turned up and make certain demands, one of the grounds of their claim being that the Deputy Superintendent General had not authority to cancel and that notification had not been properly sent them, although they had been notified at their last known address. Then we have the other complicated case where those agreements are sold to or traded in with other parties and we do not know who may have an interest in them. We have no notification of their interest until after cancellation proceedings take place; then the other parties suddenly turn up with an interest in the property and say that they have not been notified. These are the cases that we want to cover in this section.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister has made
very clear why the first part is necessary, and in that I cordially support him. He has not, however, made clear to me the second part, because if these men are not on the record < f the department as purchasers from a purchaser or otherwise they are not entitled to any notice, and though they might hang around here until doomsday the minister would be justified in ignoring them. He does not need the section for this purpose; there must be some other.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am advised by the Justice department that with respect co one case the best thing we can do is to return the money, although we did all we thought was necessary to cover the case.
The question is involved there of the Deputy Superintendent General's authority, as well as the matter of notification and a second party appearing in the transaction.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If an official is charged
with the performance of a duty before a right can be cancelled, there is no good reason why that duty should not be performed literally and practically in accordance with the statute. The difficulty with the government and' with most public bodies is found in the slipshod work of officials who come to think that anything will do. It is quite right that there should be some notice.
I do not think any one wishes to put the law in the position that my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) suggests it would be by this amendment, whereby cancellation could be made without notice of any kind. Very often the courts act without notifying every one in interest. They take what is called a representative of a class, and it is held that where a given class of people have the same sort of interest, service of a notice upon any one of that class is sufficient. A great deal of property is dealt with in that way. The minister might add some provision that the notification, however irregular in form it might be, would be good provided it had1 been given in accordance with the rules to some one of the class of persons who have an actual interest. But I do not think there ought to be an entire dispensing with any effort to let people know that it is intended to deal with their rights. That ought to be preserved to some extent, though I am willing to facilitate as much as possible the main objects the minister has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have no
desire that the rights of the purchaser or lessee shall not be protected.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But your section destroys all protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This section is not so much for the future as it is for the past. I agree that for the future we might curtail it to a definite procedure, and that I am willing to do. But here we have cases where the officials acted in good faith, not at all in a slipshod manner, as my hon. friend suggests. Cancellation proceedings have always been preceded by an attempt to locate the person concerned and notify him of the condition in which his contract stood. The main object is to prevent any doubt arising as to the validity of what has happened in the past.
Indian Act Amendment

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That could be done by a few simple words.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We might
argue for hours about this. The best thing we can do is to take it back and have it redrafted.
Section stands.
On section 5-Power of Governor in Council over expenditure of capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This is to
widen the scope within which we may spend band funds for the purchase of implements or machinery, also to provide for the expenditure of capital moneys standing at the credit of the band upon such improvements or works as will when completed properly represent capital, or as the section goes on to say-
-in the making of loans to members of the band to promote progress, no such loan, however, to exceed in amount one-half of the appraised value of the interest of the borrower in the lands held by him.
Almost eveiy day I have complaints arising out of a rather vicious system that prevails in the Indian department, and that is the agent has authority in case of distress or necessity to authorize the Indian to purchase horses, machinery and equipment in order that he may carry on his farming operations. Members from the prairie provinces have been complaining to me almost every day that these accounts have not been paid. I hope to try and limit this practice to cases of absolute distress; that is, the agent will not have authority to issue these permits except in case of absolute want or distress; and to take the place of that I want to make it a little easier to secure capital moneys for the purpose of assisting the Indians to get started. We have a profit on the greater production scheme of some $60,000, which has been turned into the treasury, and I am going to ask in a supplementary estimate for that sum to be revoted to assist in this very purpose, in order that we may stop this practice of the Indians purchasing from implement companies, from merchants and from farmers stock and the necessary equipment to carry on their farming operations. We will utilize that amount, and in addition the capital funds we have now to the credit of the band, for this purpose.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I see no objection to this section. I think those additions are probably in the interest of the Indians. I do not quite follow the minister, though, on the other phase, namely that relating to the $60,000 which he proposes having in the estimates.
Is that greater production money?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is profits from the greater production scheme. Under the act we have to pay it into the treasury, and I am asking for it as a grant for the very purpose set out here, in order that we will be able to loan the Indian money rather than have him go to the merchant and get into debt, with all the trouble that involves.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I want the minister to
understand I am not objecting to the section at all; I think it is all right, but when this money is voted is the minister going to allow it to be applied to any cases of the past where agents have authorized purchases where they should not have-in payment of notes given, for example?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There are cases now where band funds have been used for this very purpose. Of course, the band have always loaned the money. It is the clearing up of all indebtedness I have reference to, but there is no authority for me to do it under the act. I want to try and stop this vicious practice if I can.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think the minister got my point. I emphasize again, the section is right, to enable the minister to advance money for machinery out of band funds, but when he votes the money he speaks of, is he going to permit any of it to be used, not to purchase new machinery or horses or to make a new loan for the Indian's immediate purposes, but rather to pay past debts incurred by the Indians and never before recognized by the department? If he is, well, there is opportunity for frightful favouritism, and I think the minister would be in hot water from the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I confess I
have a lot of difficulty to know how to straighten these matters out; but no, it is not my intention to use that money for that purpose. What I actually want this money for is to start the younger men farming. My hon. friend knows that when a young man graduates from one of these schools, if he can be induced to marry and settle down, he usually makes a pretty good farmer, but we have no funds from which to loan him money to make a start, and I propose asking for this $60,000 to be revoted to be used for that purpose.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say none of this money would be available for wiping out past debts?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Not the
money we are discussing now, that is the profits from the greater production scheme.

Indian Act Amendment

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But there will be otlher
provision made for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If the minister ever intends to apply money to those purposes, I hope he will give me a chance to put in an application on behalf of very many clients.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It would be a rather dangerous thing to do.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have seen the minister
several times about these debts that have been incurred by the Indians, some of them three and four and five years old. I did not intend to take any part in this discussion, but from the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition it would rather seem to me that he objects to these old debts being paid.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I object to paying them.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In that case I think I should refer to the matter. Many of these debts have been incurred as long ago as three and four years. Goods have been sold to the Indians on the signed order of the agent, as agent. Horses, goods from the store, and in some cases oil from the oil tanks have been purchased, not at fictitious prices at all, but on the signed order of the agent, as agent, and when these men delivered their goods' to the Indians on the strength of the order signed by the agent, as agent, they certainly felt the government was behind the agent and would see that the bills were paid. Now, after waiting for years, and crops having failed-in one case as the minister knows, a man was burnt out and lost his store and stock, involving a loss of some thirty or forty thousand dollars-if there is any money available I think it should be devoted to wiping out these old debts. I know it is a difficult matter, and I believe the minister is using his very best energies to meet the difficulty and to get the old debts paid, but some of the Indians have died, and others have moved away and feel as though they were paying for a dead horse; they are not willing to make the effort. I think there is no possibility of having these debts paid unless the government takes the matter in hand and pays the debts itself.
I do not think the government can afford to be so unjust as to see a man take the goods off his shelf for the Indians on the strength of an order signed by the agent, as agent, and then say: We will not pay those debts.
I do not think the government can afford to do that. It is setting an example, I was going to say, of dishonesty. I think there is a moral obligation on the government to wipe these debts out, and I think now would be a proper time for the minister to say just how far he has been able to proceed. He has been trying to meet this difficulty he has told me, and has been doing his utmost in that direction, and I have no complaint to make on that score. He has also been in touch with the Indian Commissioner for the purpose of providing a remedy, and perhaps it would be a satisfaction to those who are expecting some remuneration if the minister would make a statement on the subject so that we would know just where we are.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This is, of course, one of the very difficult problems that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs has to face. I point out to my hon. friend that there are faults on both sides. Very frequently the Indians are somewhat easy to persuade that they require horses, implements and food when, perhaps, they do not require them at all; and through the easy methods pursued by the agents obligations were incurred that never should have been entered into at all.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
What authority had the
agent to endorse these purchases from time to time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The agent
simply issues an order.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Had he authority to do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
On this
order the agent says he thinks the Indian worthy of credit. Of course I take no exception to the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Millar): there is undoubtedly an obligation on Ithe part of ithe government through their agents. I have now put a stop to that sort of thing, and confined the relief to cases of dire necessity. What I want to do is to stop the practice and try and clean up this indebtedness that exists in practically all of the provinces. I may say that in the province of Alberta we have the matter pretty well in hand; but in Saskatchewan, for some reason or another-I imagine very largely owing to the bad crops and to the conditions that surround the farmers generally-the Indians, as well as

Indian Act Amendment
other farmers have been unable to pay their indebtedness. If we have a good agent, and after all that is the greatest asset you could have on a reserve, we will not be very long in cleaning these matters up, except in some particularly aggravated cases. We are endeavouring first to secure the consent of the band for the purpose of liquidating this indebtedness. Undoubtedly before it is finished we will require some assistance in the cleaning-up operations, because as my hon. friend has pointed out in many cases the Indian has died, or otherwise disappeared, and the indebtedness stands. However, I think it will have a good effect if we cease doing that kind of business altogether because there is a temptation on the part of people who have articles to sell to induce the Indian to buy if they can, persuading him that something of the character indicated is needed. The indebtedness is incurred in that way when probably the Indian would be far better off if he were not given assistance it all. That is usually what has happened in the most aggravated cases. However, we are making a real effort bo clean up the Saskatchewan situation. It is probably the worst, and it is confined to three or four reserves. The reserve my hon. friend has in his constituency at Broadview is one, the reserve at Touchwood is another, and there are a few other cases which need immediate attention. We hope to be able to clean the entire situation up without having to come to the government for assistance except for a very small amount.	*

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think what the minister
has said may be true in some parts of Saskatchewan. I could not say positively that there are no cases in the reserve at Broadview, but I know of none. I do know however that in many cases goods were sold that were absolutely needed, goods off the shelf. The man that I spoke of who has the largest account-$6,000 or $5,500-took the goods right from the shelf. I think it would be well if the minister could see some way to use part of this or some other money, to pay part of this obligation in cash immediately, because many of the persons concerned are in dire need and even a settlement at once of a part of the obligation would be a great help. I would ask the minister to give this matter his very best consideration. The district is one where the crop has failed; we have had poor crops for some three or four years, and most of these people are very much in need.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am not objecting to
the payment, but I warn the minister first that he will be in difficulty if he starts this tiling because the number is almost legion. I know myself of many cases-many large and many small-and I protest against any system of picking out a few and providing money to pay them out of the treasury. If the minister is going to pay them all right, but let him come down with a vote for the whole amount; it is the only fair way to do. Section agreed to.
On section 6-Procedure where wife living apart.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We have
cases where wives have left their husbands and are living in the United States, and it is not desirable that they should be enfranchised along with their husbands. That is why we are asking for this provision.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Enfranchisement of Indians, section 122a revived.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The difficulty here is, the Justice department have informed us that although section 122a is retained in the act it is doubtful if it was not cancelled in the amendments of 1920. We are reviving section 122a and making it clear that it remains.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is section 122a?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is set out here; it is in the old act. This is to make it absolutely clear that the section was not struck out in the amendments of 1920.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The explanatory note
does not say what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I will read
the section:
If an Indian who holds no land in a reserve, does not reside on a reserve and does not follow the Indian mode of life, makes application to be enfranchised, and satisfies the Superintendent General that he is self-supporting and fit to be enfranchised, and surrenders all claims whatsoever to any interest in the lands of the band to which he belongs, and accepts his share of the funds at the credit of the band including the principal of the annuities of the band, to which share he would have been entitled had he been enfranchised under the foregoing sections of the act, in full of all claims to the property of the band, or in case the band to which he belongs has no funds or principal of annuities, surrenders all claim whatsoever to any property of the band, the Governor in Council may order that such Indian be enfranchised and pay his said share if any, and from the date of such order such Indian, together with his wife and unmarried minor children, shall be held to be enfranchised.

Indian Act Amendment

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Has the minister the
section of 1920?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, I have
not.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Could the minister give the general effect of i't?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, I have
not the old act here. The purpose is to make it absolutely clear that that section was not cancelled in 1920.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I know it was not the
intention to cancel it. The reason I ask is that the minister came down in 9 p.m. 1922 with some further amendments and I was never very enthusiastic about them. Is the minister quite clear it was not the 1922 amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes. The
J922 amendments as my right hon. friend will remember, cancelled some of the drastic yowers of the Superintendent General, but they did not interfere with the mode of enfranchisement. The amendment of 1922 was that the enfranchisement should not be carried out without the knowledge of the band. This affected the whole of 122a, so the Justice department said.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The enfranchisement
should not be carried out without the consent of the band, and consequently the effect would be to repeal section 122a. I think it is the 1922 section that does the repealing, but it does not matter. We want it restored, and I am satisfied to do that. Does the minister say that it is working out well to have the band virtually in control of the enfranchisement, as was brought about by him in 1922?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We are not having any difficulty.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: How many is the minister enfranchising?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A very considerable number. A' return was brought down fifteen days after the opening of the session. There was only one band, the Six Nations band, which raised any particular objection. The enfranchisement is still going on amongst the Indians, and I think I am safe in saying that it is working out satisfactorily.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My understanding is
that, at the rate at which we are going, the enfranchisement is very slow and that our grandchildren will be in their graves and
several generations after them 'before the Indians are citizens. Was it not a mistake to pay so much attention to a recalcitrant band in Brantford county? It does not seem to have mollified them very much. They seem to be going to the League of Nations over our heads.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: One of the complaints was that we were enfranchising them against their will.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The minister has explained the meaning of sections 107 and 122a, and he has given us to understand that a number of Indians have been enfranchised under the provisions of those sections, although he does not seem to be clear as to exactly how many have been enfranchised in the last year or two. He has told us that the tribe has to give its consent before an Indian is enfranchised. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, if an enfranchised Indian has common, communal property in the band; otherwise, no.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: To what extent does the enfranchisement of an Indian make him a Canadian citizen?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
He is a
Canadian citizen before enfranchisement, but he has not the full right of citizenship, namely the privilege of using a ballot.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: After enfranchisement, is it not the case that he has every right that we possess except that he is not a member of parliament?

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is just what I wanted to find out. Am I to understand that after the Indian has been enfranchised according to this legislation, he may vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The full
right of citizenship.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In that case, will the Elections Act be amended to provide for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is not necessary.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, because the Elections Act merely exempts Indians who are wards. He is no longer a ward; he has all the rights of citizenship. He can even take a drink if he can get it by law.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Have the provisions referred to under section 7 the effect of breaking up the bands or the tribes, perhaps before they are fit for citizenship? Does the minister believe that this is working well?
Indian Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There is no doubt about that. There are in Canada a great number of Indians who are educated in the various schools that are provided for them and there is no reason why they should not have the full right of citizenship. The trouble arose over the fact that the Superintendent General had power, without the consent of the band to enfranchise an Indian and demand his share of the communal property. If the Indian has not a communal interest in the band, the band has nothing to say about the matter. He has free will as regards that. He himself makes application always for enfranchisement.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
How many Indians have
been given the right to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at the return that was brought down, he will find out how many were enfranchised last year. When the estimates are brought down, I shall be glad to furnish that information if necessary.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-Trespassing on reserves or cutting or removing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This is
simply to assist in the better preservation of timber and other property of the band and to provide penalties for the destruction of such property.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Does this mean that any man who buys hay from an Indian living on a reserve will have to have a license from the Superintendent General before he can deal with the Indian in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Not necessarily. He can get a license from the local agent or secure permission of the council. This is to provide penalties when destruction takes place when no permission of any 6ort is given.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will it be necessary for a buyer of hay to have a license for every Indian he trades with or just a general license to do business with the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Just a general license issued by the agent in charge, which would always be by consent of the council.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This would not cover the case of an Indian who drives a load of hay from the reserve to a neighbouring tcwn and offers that hay for sale?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No. That is his own property.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
One needs to study these provisions carefully to be certain what they mean. Reading this section over, I am of the opinion that it goes too far. I think the minister has a section under which nobody could sell anything off a reserve. It reads:
Every person, or Indian, other than an Indian of the band to which the reserve belongs, who, without the license in writing of the Superintendent General or of some officer or person deputed by him for that purpose, cuts, carries away or removes from any of the lands, roads or allowances for roads in a reserve, any of the trees, saplings, shrubs, underwood, timber, cordwood, or part of a tree, or hay, or removes any of the stone, soil, minerals, metals or other valuables from the said land, roads or allowances for roads, or who buys any of the above-mentioned materials, shall, on summary conviction thereof before any stipendiary magistrate. .	. .
And so forth, be liable. If an Indian on the reserve takes his hay into town and this section passes, nobody can buy that hay unless he has a license to do so. Does the minister intend that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That the
purchaser should have to have a license?

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is not intended.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the result.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It must be an Indian of the band to which the reserve belongs.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is to
stop the destruction. In most cases it is wood that is pilfered off these reserves. You require to have a fairly broad provision. Nearly all these men, when they dispose of their produce, have authority from the agent to dispose of it. If it were otherwise the Indian would never keep any money at all. It would be all dissipated. You have to have some control of the Indians, or they would never have a dollar to pay their debts. They would sell their stuff, it would be gone, and that would be the end of it. This is to stop that sort of thing. It may look drastic in the case of a good Indian who is a law-abiding citizen, but you have to make laws for those who are not law-abiding, who will get all the money they can, pauperize themselves by selling everything; their families will get into trouble and the department have to come to their rescue. This measure is intended to cover cases of that kind and to prevent pilfering.

Indian Act Amendment

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does the minister mean
that no man is able to contract with an Indian to take from that Indian's lands trees or shrubbery or anything else which the agent does not wish the Indian to sell?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But the agent authorizes the Indian to sell his hay, and the Indian comes to town, and no one can buy that hay unless he has a license.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, that
is not the intention.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the way the act reads.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If he purchases without the Indian being able to show his authority to sell then you can prosecute.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the way it should be, but that is not the way it reads.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No. Nobody can buy,
unless he has a license, any hay grown on the Indian's land. If the man who buys is an Indian of the band, he is permitted to buy, but if not he cannot buy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If the Indian was not in possession of authority from the agent to sell, he should not buy from him.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Even suppose he has
authority to sell the hay by license, then the purchaser is not protected according to this section. As a matter of fact, if the Indian is a member of the band he does not need any license at all to sell the hay under this section. It is only one who is not of the band who has to have a license to sell, and very rightly so. But I am assuming now that the man who is selling has a right to sell. The fellow who takes the hay to town has the right to sell it. The minister is preventing anybody buying it under this section. There is no use giving a man a right to sell if everybody is prevented from buying.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member contend that a man must have a license to buy?

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the drafting.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The section reads:
Every person .... who, without the license in
writing of the Superintendent General, or of some
officer or person deputed by him for that purpose,
cuts, carries away or removes from any of the lands
roads or allowances for roads in a reserve, .... or who buys any of the above-mentioned materials shall on summary conviction thereof before any stipendiary magistrate, police magistrate or any two justices of the peace or an Indian agent, incur in each case the cost of prosecution-

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the section
is poorly drafted, but if I were called upon to interpret that section I would interpret it in this way:
-or who buys from someone who has not a license or who is not otherwise authorized-
And so on. I agree with the leader of the opposition that it is not as clearly expressed as it should be, but I think he has put a darker construction upon it than the circumstances of the case really merit.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I will have this section examined as well as the others.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What do the woftls " or other valuables aforesaid " mean? Does that include live stock?

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think it would include live stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
What is
involved in the section is definitely se( out. It does not mention live stock.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It says " other valuables as
aforesaid."

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would the minister say
that this clause is drafted in such a way that there is no ambiguity about it? The reserves with which I am familiar are not very far from towns of considerable size, and it is a common practice for men to come to town with loads of hay. I have purchased it from them myself. I do not know whether they had a license or not. I may have been liable without knowing it. I think a great many others have bought hay from them without inquiring whether the man had a license or not, and probably did not think he required a license.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The hon.
member was not liable.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If the clause means what
the right hon. leader of the opposition thinks it means, we might be liable.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have no doubt what it means, but if this clause passes in its present form, it does not matter whether the Indian has a license to sell or not. The buyer would require to have a license.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is an extreme interpretation.

Land Titles Act Amendment

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not want the minister to report to the Minister of Justice that I have said that the clause is badly drafted. I think it is very clear, but it means the wrong thing.

maintopic: INDIAN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would like to answer the leader of the opposition. The clause is not intended to mean what he says it clearly means. In that respect it is not drafted to meet the desires of the government and of the minister in charge.
Progress reported.

maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 188, to amend the Land Titles Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Qualification of registrar and deputy.
, Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil): This section is simply to permit us to utilize the gold commissioner, who is not a barrister, for the purpose of registering.

maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext: I never knew there was a Land Titles Act for the Dominion. Does it apply just to the Territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext: To the Territories and the Yukon.

maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would not the law as
to resgistration be included in the Yukon Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think not. This amendment is simply to allow us to use ;he gold commissioner, who is not a barrister, :or the purpose of registering all claims that require registration.

maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext: Not mining claims?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext: Transfers of real property.
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Shall I report the bill?
,Mr. MEIGHEN:	I have no objection to
the present gold commissioner being appointed as registrar; he would be quite capable; but does the minister consider it advisable to make the repeal applicable generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It applies
only to the Territories and the Yukon.

maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I know that.
[Mr. McMaster.J

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: LAND TITLES ACT-AMENDMENT
